d.title: The keyword sanitiser, measured on both populations
d.caption: Almost everyone writes this filter first, and it is worth measuring on **both** populations — because a filter tested only against attacks looks fine. Against attacks it catches 3 of 10. Against benign input it blocks 6 of 8. That is **precision 0.33 and recall 0.30**: it misses most attacks while rejecting most legitimate users, which is the worst of both outcomes and the reason this layer is close to worthless on its own.

d.title: Six layers, and only one of them is structural
d.caption: The ordering matters because effort distributes badly here. Teams spend weeks on the first row — **measured at 0.33 precision** — and minutes on the last, which is the only one that converts a successful injection into a *failed action*. Every other layer makes damage less likely; least privilege on tools makes it impossible, and that difference is the whole security argument.

d.title: Indirect injection: the user is not the attacker
d.caption: Direct injection is someone typing an override into a chat box. **Indirect** injection is instructions arriving in content the system retrieved — a web page, an email, a support ticket, a document in the corpus, a tool result. It is worse on every axis: the user may be a victim rather than the attacker, filtering is harder because you cannot reject every retrieved document containing imperative sentences, and the surface grows with every capability that reads external content. What helps is the same conclusion as §03 from a different direction: treat retrieved content as untrusted **at the action boundary**, not the text boundary.

d.title: One checklist item is a precondition for the other six
d.caption: Knowing **which prompt produced which output** is not one item among seven — it is the one the rest depend on. Without it a quality change cannot be attributed, a rollback cannot be verified, and an A/B test has no data at all. It costs one field on the response and one column in the log, and it is routinely the thing missing when a team cannot explain why last month was better.

nodes.label: Rollback becomes verifiable
nodes.sub: you can see it took effect

nodes.label: Without it, none of the three

d.title: Git gives you five of these for free; the registry trades one away
d.caption: Files in git give review, history, rollback and atomicity with the code for nothing and with no new system. The row that is the **real** trade is the fifth: in git the prompt and the parser that reads its output move together, and in a registry they do not — so a prompt change can land without the code change that handles it. The case for a registry arrives when people who cannot deploy need to change prompts, which is a genuine situation and not a tooling preference.

d.title: Halt on error rate and latency, not on quality
d.caption: Note what the automatic halt condition uses. **Quality takes longer to measure than an hour** — 2.12 measured how much longer — so wiring a rollout's kill switch to a quality metric means it either never fires or fires on noise. Error rate and latency move within minutes and are unambiguous, so they catch the catastrophic cases; the quality decision is made deliberately, later, once there is enough data to support it.

d.caption: Five are essential, and two are not prompt management at all. The second row carries the only real condition — an A/B framework is essential **at volume** and overkill below it, because 2.12's sample sizes say a low-traffic A/B cannot resolve the differences you would be running it to find. The last two rows belong to other lessons, and saying so keeps the checklist honest rather than long.

d.title: Same four components; the weight moves
d.caption: Laid side by side the six templates have an identical structure and differ only in **which component carries the task**. That is what makes the collection useful as a diagnostic rather than a library: identify which component your task leans on, and the failure in the right-hand column tells you what you will get if you underwrite it. Three of the six lean on *context*, which is the component most often left implicit.

d.title: Four questions that produce the template
d.caption: These generate a prompt rather than requiring you to find one that fits, which is why they are more useful than the six worked examples — **a template's generic parts are exactly the parts you have to replace**. The fourth is the one most often skipped, and it is mandatory rather than optional whenever the input might simply not contain the answer.

d.title: Six separators, everything else held constant
d.caption: "Models are sensitive to wording" is agreed with and not acted on, so here is a number. Three separators score **6 of 6** and `a means b` scores **1 of 6** — on an identical task with identical examples. The rank column shows this is not a cliff: under `means` the right answer sits at rank 2 or 3 on five of six items, so the model understands the task and something else is winning. What is winning is the pattern — `a means b` is ordinary English that continues many ways, where `a -> b` is a format.

d.title: Standard advice, applied, and catastrophic
d.caption: The table's first row says to move an instruction to the end when it is not being followed — grounded advice, since recency helps in long contexts. Applied to a working few-shot prompt it went from **6 of 6 to 0 of 6**. And the third row is the one that explains it: with *no* instruction at all the prompt scores 6 of 6, so the instruction was never doing the work. In a few-shot prompt the model is continuing a **pattern** whose final line is the query awaiting its answer, and an instruction placed after that line breaks the pattern exactly where it matters.

d.title: The debugging procedure, reordered by cost
d.caption: The usual seven steps are all reasonable, and their usual order is the order people think of them — which is not the order of cost. Reordered, the first two are nearly free and catch the most common causes: **2.1's incident was three weeks spent on prompt versions for a truncation that was visible in the rendered request.** Changing the prompt is last, because the alternative to measuring is 31 noise-driven changes over 18 months.
